questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Verbal irony ahead of the character
questions.learningObjective: Explain where verbal irony sits when the claim comes first
questions.stem: I noticed the diver says the water is perfectly safe moments before the alarm sounds; explain what the play is doing there.

answer.exemplar: The line places the diver's confidence ahead of the information that will contradict it, so the audience holds a promise the play is about to break. Because the claim arrives before the danger is real rather than after, the irony is directed forward, and the audience waits for the moment when the statement will be shown to be false. The character's certainty becomes the measure of the coming alarm, and the scene's tension grows from the gap between what is said and what the audience already knows is coming.

questions.explanation: Putting the confident claim before the alarm gives the audience a promise the play will break, so the irony runs forward and the tension grows. Saying it after the fact would only make the character look foolish.
questions.hint: Consider when the claim is made relative to the alarm.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A stage version and what it changes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a revision to the order of scenes changes
questions.stem: I read a revised script where the storm warning moved from the second act to the first; explain what the revision changes.

answer.exemplar: Moving the warning earlier changes the meaning of everything that follows, because the audience now watches every later scene as people who have been warned. The same lines of dialogue carry a different charge, since the characters' ignorance is now the audience's knowledge, and the play's worry shifts from whether the danger will be recognised to how long the recognition is delayed. What the revision cannot change is the printed page: the words the actors speak and the shape of the plot remain, so the difference between the versions is a difference in expectation rather than in events.

questions.explanation: Moving the warning earlier makes the audience informed before the characters are, so the same lines carry a different charge and the suspense shifts to delay. The events and words are unchanged, so only expectation differs.
questions.hint: Consider what the audience now knows that they did not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A device claim the text contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a contradicted claim does to the play's world
questions.stem: I noted the programme's claim that the play contains no supernatural events; explain what a contradicted claim can do.

answer.exemplar: A contradicted claim can put the play's world in dispute, because the claim is part of what the audience was told to expect and the text has refused it. If the programme insists that nothing supernatural appears and the scene then shows the diver speaking to a presence no one else can see, the audience has to decide which account governs: the printed promise or the evidence of the stage. questions.explanation: A contradicted claim puts the play's world in dispute, so the audience must decide whether the promise or the stage governs. It differs from an error in the paperwork, because it gives the audience a rule to test.

questions.stem: I asked what changed when the tank broke in the stage version instead of the man falling; explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: The change relocates the accident from a person's body to the apparatus, and everything the audience reads through the event shifts with it. When the man falls, the scene is about his carelessness, his pain, and the question of who was watching; when the tank breaks, the fault is distributed through the equipment, the schedule, and the room, and the flooding reaches everyone at once. The stakes become collective rather than personal, so the mischief is no longer confined to the one who slips, and the scene ends by making the whole laboratory answerable. Nothing about the plot changes, but the subject of the scene does.

questions.explanation: Moving the accident from a fall to a broken tank makes the fault collective rather than personal, so the scene ends by making the whole laboratory answerable. The plot is unchanged but the subject of the scene is not.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a subplot supplies a second measure for the main action
questions.stem: I asked why the play keeps returning to the anemone that the transfer will cost; explain what the subplot is doing.

answer.exemplar: The anemone gives the audience a second measure against which the transfer can be judged. An audience that has caught the chorus once will listen to it differently for the rest of the play, and it will listen to the keepers and the supervisors with the same new attention, which is what makes an unreliable chorus a source of tension rather than a comic nuisance.

questions.hint: Consider what one caught error changes about the rest.

stimulus.body: The printed text states twice that no animal is ever harmed in the play. In the last scene the keeper carries the anemone out of the tank in her hands, and the curtain falls before the audience is told what happens to it.

options.text: It is an oversight, since the stage directions forgot the closing line

options.text: It puts the claim in doubt at the exact moment the audience most wants it true

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Verbal irony ahead of the character
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a small affectionate claim creates irony
questions.stem: I asked why the assistant says the tank looks lovely moments before the water goes wrong; explain the effect.

answer.exemplar: The compliment puts a claim about the world in place of the knowledge that will replace it, so the scene's irony runs on the gap between the appearance and the condition underneath. Because the remark is small and affectionate rather than confident or grandiose, the contrast is harder to see coming, and the audience may not register the coming failure until the sound changes. That delay is what gives the scene its shape: the ordinary admiration of a working object becomes the last thing the character says about it, and the audience hears the line afterwards with a different set of ears.

questions.explanation: An affectionate claim about appearance placed just before the failure creates irony that runs on the gap between surface and condition. Its smallness delays recognition, and the audience hears the line again afterwards with different ears.
questions.hint: Consider why the remark is so small and warm.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh the reading of a contradicted claim as error or as device
questions.stem: I asked whether a contradicted claim should be treated as an error or as a device; which answer fits best?

options.misconception: assumes care would forbid the claim

options.text: As a device, since any contradiction is always deliberate and always clear
options.misconception: overstates the deliberateness of the break
